sources.title: Lean Thinking and Practice
sources.author: Lean Enterprise Institute; Womack and Jones concepts
sources.reliability: high for lean definitions; not independent efficacy evidence
sources.notes: Page attributes five principles to Womack and Jones 1996; this is not inferred page publication year.
sources.access_evidence: Retrieved five principles and purpose/process/people exposition.
supported_claims: Five principles are customer value, value stream, flow, pull and continuing improvement.
Process and people are central to implementation.

sources.title: Lean Operations
sources.author: Lean Enterprise Institute
sources.reliability: high for definitions; benefit statements are practitioner claims
sources.access_evidence: Retrieved activity categories, seven wastes and flow/pull descriptions.
supported_claims: Activities can be value-added, essential nonvalue-added or waste.
Inventory and waiting are among the wastes examined.
Pull means downstream obtains what it currently needs from upstream when continuous flow is not possible.

sources.title: Introduction to Theory of Constraints
sources.author: Goldratt Research Labs
sources.reliability: high for TOC method exposition; not independent efficacy proof
sources.notes: Copyright year not treated as publication date. No claim that every complex system has a stable single physical bottleneck.
sources.access_evidence: Introduction and all five focusing steps retrieved, including repeated return to step 1 and local/global optimization discussion.
supported_claims: TOC focuses on the system constraint and whole-system goal.
Steps are identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate and repeat without inertia.

sources.title: DMAIC
sources.author: American Society for Quality
sources.reliability: high for phase definitions; not causal evaluation of a particular intervention
sources.notes: No sigma conversion or 3.4 defects claim imported.
sources.access_evidence: Retrieved overview, five phases and usage distinction for existing processes.
supported_claims: DMAIC improves existing processes missing performance or customer expectations.
Phases are define, measure, analyze, improve and control.
It can be used with Six Sigma or independently.

sources.title: The 8 Steps for Leading Change
sources.author: Kotter International
sources.reliability: high for current model definition; commercial efficacy statements not adopted as independent evidence
sources.notes: Uses current accelerators labels, explicitly distinguished from initial linear model.
sources.access_evidence: Retrieved history and eight accelerator headings with descriptions.
supported_claims: Current accelerators include urgency, coalition, vision, volunteer participation, barrier removal, wins, sustained acceleration and institutionalization.
Official model evolved from linear steps to dynamic accelerators.

sources.title: Enduring Ideas: The 7-S Framework
sources.author: McKinsey & Company; Lowell Bryan presentation
sources.reliability: high for model intent; not empirical proof of effectiveness
sources.notes: Article dated 1 March 2008. Interactive presentation itself was not played; names supplemented by ILO guide.
sources.access_evidence: Retrieved article body explaining coordination and interrelated factors without hierarchy.
supported_claims: Factors are interrelated and not organized in a simple hierarchy.

sources.title: The Effective Employers’ Organisation — Strategy guide
sources.author: International Labour Organization, Bureau for Employers’ Activities
sources.reliability: high for institutional training exposition; secondary to model originators
sources.notes: Source supplements missing seven labels in accessible McKinsey article; no claim of original 7S research.
sources.access_evidence: Official 58-page PDF retrieved; printed page 28 passage on McKinsey 7S inspected in indexed content.
supported_claims: Seven factors are strategy, structure, systems, style, staff, skills and shared values.
Guide presents alignment among factors as a way to examine strategy feasibility.

sources.title: Managing the risk of learning: Psychological safety in work teams
sources.author: Amy C. Edmondson
sources.reliability: high for construct exposition and bounded study discussion; not randomized causal proof of proposed workflow
sources.notes: Dated 15 March 2002, forthcoming handbook chapter. This is not represented as direct reading of the original 1999 article; its HBS item page returned 403.
sources.access_evidence: Official HBS 38-page paper retrieved; PDF pages 1–15 definition, distinctions, study descriptions and learning process inspected.
supported_claims: Psychological safety concerns perceived interpersonal risks such as questions, feedback and error reporting.
It differs from trust and group cohesiveness and does not imply absence of pressure.
Team learning also needs goals, coordination and reflection/action cycles.
